summary: Presents a retrieval-method YANG data model for connectionless OAM protocols. It provides technology-independent RPC operations that tools can use to ask for OAM information, and it can be extended with technology-specific details. It builds on the generic connectionless OAM model and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Think of a standard way to ask a network to report back on how it is doing. Everyone uses the same question form, so any reporting tool can understand the answer.

questions: what are continuity check and path discovery rpcs
how does yang relate to ping and traceroute
subtitle: Two on-demand YANG commands, continuity check and path discovery, for ping-and-traceroute style tools on connectionless networks.

tldr.problem: Connectionless networks have many similar OAM tools such as ping and traceroute, and each is driven differently, while retrieval procedures are expected to change faster than the data they retrieve.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a separate YANG module with two technology-independent on-demand RPC operations, continuity-check and path-discovery, which return data defined by the generic connectionless OAM model in RFC 8532.
tldr.outcome: Technology-specific OAM models can extend these RPCs, and new retrieval methods can be added later without touching the data model.

today: RFC 8533 is a Proposed Standard from April 2019 and the text shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on the generic connectionless OAM model in RFC 8532.

sections.title: Why a Separate Retrieval Model
sections.content:
OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) lets operators monitor communications, troubleshoot failures and monitor service levels and performance. Ping and Traceroute (RFC 4443) and Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (RFC 5880) are well-known fault verification and isolation tools for IP networks, and other technologies built similar toolsets.

RFC 8533 defines an on-demand retrieval method YANG model for OAM protocols that use connectionless communication. It is split out from the generic connectionless OAM model in RFC 8532 so that the retrieved data and the retrieval procedures are not mixed. The RFC expects retrieval procedures to evolve faster than the data model, and new procedures can then be defined for the same data.
sections.eli5: The list of facts about the network lives in one place, and the way you ask for those facts lives in another. That way the questions can change without rewriting the facts.

sections.title: Two Generic RPC Operations
sections.content:
The model works through remote procedure calls sent to a NETCONF server, meaning the device that needs to execute the OAM command, and returns a response. The module ietf-connectionless-oam-methods summarizes common OAM functions as two generic RPCs: continuity-check and path-discovery. They are run on demand and map onto technology-specific tools from RFC 7276. For the IP OAM model, continuity check corresponds to IP Ping and path discovery to IP Traceroute.

These RPCs are a base building block. They are meant to be extended with technology-specific parameters to derive models for, for example, ICMP Ping or Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping (RFC 8029). That is why the RPCs sit in their own module.

Each RPC is available only if the matching feature from the RFC 8532 module is supported.
sections.eli5: There are two basic questions a tool can ask: 'can I reach it?' and 'what route do I take to get there?'. These are the same ideas as ping and traceroute.

sections.title: Inputs and Outputs
sections.content:
Both RPCs share a grouping of input parameters: a destination test point (whose address grouping comes from the RFC 8532 module), a mandatory source interface and outbound interface, and an optional VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding instance). The continuity check also takes a session type, which must be on demand if given, a packet count (default 5), a ttl (default 255) and a packet-size in octets (range 64 to 10000, default 64).

The outputs reuse data groupings from the RFC 8532 module (continuity-check-data and path-discovery-data). Each response also carries a protocol ID, optional protocol metadata (for example the Internet Protocol number), a status code and a status sub-code. Path discovery returns a list of responses with a response-index.
sections.eli5: You tell the tool where to start, where to aim and how many test messages to send. It answers with who replied and whether the test passed.

sections.title: Status Codes and Identities
sections.content:
The module defines identities so that results are comparable across technologies. The base status codes, taken from the reachability and path verification ideas in RFC 7276, are success-reach, fail-reach, success-path-verification and fail-path-verification. Two sub-codes give more detail: invalid-cc and invalid-pd, for an invalid Continuity Check message or path discovery message.

Protocol IDs identify what ran the test. The module defines identities for Internet protocols, proprietary protocols, Service Function Chaining, MPLS, MPLS-TP, TWAMP and BIER. If a technology needs its own codes, such as ICMP error codes from RFC 4443 for a ping, it can define them in its own model.
sections.eli5: Each answer comes with a result label like 'reached' or 'not reached', plus an optional reason. The labels are the same for every kind of network.

sections.title: Extending the Methods
sections.content:
Appendix A shows two kinds of extension. The first augments the continuity-check output with ping round-trip statistics: a container with minimum, maximum and average RTT values.

The second sketches new retrieval procedures for the same data. It shows persistent retrieval: first retrieve a persistent ID based on the destination test point, then retrieve the export details. Data could be exported with IPFIX (RFC 7011) or YANG-Push. The module there is an illustration rather than a real definition, and it does not follow every guideline in RFC 8407.
sections.eli5: You can add extra boxes to the answer form, such as how long a reply took. You can also invent new ways to ask, and the facts stay the same.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The module is accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040), with SSH and TLS as the mandatory-to-implement secure transports, and access can be limited with NACM (RFC 8341).

The two RPC operations, continuity-check and path-discovery, may be sensitive in some environments, so access to them should be controlled. Unauthorized access to the data they retrieve may be used for network reconnaissance or lead to denial-of-service attacks on both the local device and the network.

IANA registered the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-connectionless-oam-methods and the YANG module ietf-connectionless-oam-methods with prefix cloam-methods.
sections.eli5: Asking the network to run tests should only be allowed for trusted people. Otherwise someone could use the answers to spy on the network or bury it in test traffic.
